hero.heading: Why Every Airline Needs a Flight Data Monitoring (FDM) Programme
hero.summary: Flight Data Monitoring is one of the most effective tools available to airline safety managers — converting recorded flight data into actionable safety insights, SOP compliance monitoring and fuel efficiency improvements. This guide explains what FDM is, why it is required, and how to establish an effective programme.

sections.heading: What Is Flight Data Monitoring?
sections.body: Flight Data Monitoring (FDM) — also known as Flight Operational Quality Assurance (FOQA) in North America — is the systematic analysis of recorded flight data to identify safety risks, monitor SOP compliance and improve operational efficiency. FDM programmes analyse data recorded by the Quick Access Recorder (QAR) or Flight Data Recorder (FDR), covering hundreds of flight parameters including airspeed, altitude, pitch, roll, engine parameters, control inputs and system states. Analysis identifies exceedances of defined thresholds, unstable approaches, hard landings, SOP deviations and fuel-efficiency opportunities. A well-run FDM programme gives safety and operations teams the objective evidence they need to identify risk, monitor trends and take corrective action before incidents occur.

sections.heading: Is FDM Mandatory for Airlines?
sections.body: Yes. ICAO Annex 19 requires commercial air transport operators of aeroplanes with a maximum certificated take-off weight exceeding 27,000 kg to establish an FDM programme as part of their Safety Management System (SMS). Many national aviation authorities — including the GCAA in the UAE — have implemented this requirement in their national regulations. Some authorities also require FDM for smaller aircraft types. Airlines that do not have an effective FDM programme are not only non-compliant with ICAO standards — they are also missing one of the most powerful tools available for proactive safety management.

sections.heading: What FDM Data Reveals
sections.body: FDM data reveals patterns and trends that are invisible without systematic analysis. Common findings include: unstable approaches (aircraft not stabilised at the required height before landing); hard landings (vertical acceleration exceeding limits); SOP deviations (crew not following standard operating procedures); engine exceedances (parameters exceeding limits during take-off or climb); and fuel-efficiency opportunities (sub-optimal profiles, excessive taxi fuel, APU usage). Individual events may be minor — but trends across the fleet reveal systemic issues that require corrective action. A single unstable approach may be unremarkable; a pattern of unstable approaches on a specific route or by a specific crew group requires investigation.

sections.heading: FDM and Fuel Efficiency
sections.body: FDM data reveals fuel-efficiency opportunities that are invisible without systematic analysis. Common opportunities include: sub-optimal climb and descent profiles; excessive taxi fuel use; opportunities for reduced-thrust take-offs; Continuous Descent Operations (CDO) compliance; and APU usage patterns. Airlines that actively use FDM for fuel management typically achieve measurable reductions in fuel burn per flight. Fuel is typically an airline's largest cost — even small percentage improvements in fuel efficiency translate into significant cost savings at scale. AeroExpert advises airlines on using FDM data for fuel efficiency improvement as part of a broader flight operations optimisation programme.

sections.heading: Establishing an Effective FDM Programme
sections.body: An effective FDM programme requires: data acquisition (QAR/FDR data collection, ground station connectivity and data transfer to the analysis platform); event definitions (exceedance thresholds, parameter limits and safety events aligned to aircraft type, operations and regulatory requirements); validation (data quality, event triggering accuracy and system configuration); analysis (systematic flight data analysis identifying exceedances, trends and safety-relevant patterns); safety review (findings presented to the safety review board, events classified by severity, corrective action priorities determined); corrective action (training interventions, procedure changes or technical rectification); trending (event rates and safety KPIs monitored over time); and management reporting (regular reports communicating FDM programme performance to accountable managers). AeroExpert supports airlines at all stages of FDM programme establishment and improvement.

sections.heading: FDM and ICAO Annex 19 Alignment
sections.body: ICAO Annex 19 requires airlines to integrate FDM into their Safety Management System. This means FDM findings must feed into the SMS hazard identification and risk assessment process, corrective actions must be tracked through the SMS, and FDM programme performance must be reported to accountable managers. Many airlines run FDM as a standalone programme disconnected from the SMS — this limits its effectiveness and creates compliance risk. AeroExpert advises on FDM-SMS integration and ICAO Annex 19 alignment for airlines in the UAE and Middle East.

faq.q: What is the difference between FDM and FOQA?
faq.a: FDM and FOQA refer to the same concept — the systematic use of recorded flight data for safety and operational improvement. FDM is the term used in ICAO documentation and by European and Middle Eastern operators; FOQA is the term used in North America.
